summary: I-JSON (Internet JSON) is a restricted profile of JSON designed to maximize interoperability and increase confidence that software can process it successfully with predictable results. It is meant to be used by protocols that want JSON to behave the same way everywhere.

plainLanguage.summary: JSON can be written in ways different programs read differently. I-JSON is a stricter set of rules so everyone reads it the same.

questions: how is i-json different from json
how should i-json encode large integers
subtitle: A strict profile of JSON that closes the loopholes where different programs read the same text differently.

tldr.problem: JSON as defined in RFC 7159 allows idioms and text encodings that different parsers handle differently, especially when data is mapped automatically into programming-language structures or database records.
tldr.mechanism: I-JSON is a JSON text with extra constraints: UTF-8 only, no surrogate or noncharacter code points, numbers limited to what IEEE 754 double precision can carry, and no duplicate member names in an object.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can reject messages that break the rules instead of guessing, and protocol designers get a predictable base for Internet protocols, including those with special security needs.

today: RFC 7493 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2015. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why a Profile of JSON
sections.content:
RFC 7159 describes JSON, which is widely used in Internet protocols. For historical reasons it allows language idioms and text encoding patterns that are likely to cause interoperability problems and software breakage. The trouble is worst when a program receiving JSON uses automated software to map it into native programming-language structures or database records.

I-JSON (short for Internet JSON) is the answer. The unit of definition is the I-JSON message. Every I-JSON message is also a JSON text as defined in RFC 7159, but with extra constraints that enforce the good interoperability practices RFC 7159 already describes. The terms object, member, array, number, name and string keep their RFC 7159 meanings, and the key words MUST, SHOULD and so on follow RFC 2119.
sections.plainLanguage: JSON lets you write the same idea in several slightly different ways, and computers can get confused. I-JSON picks the safe ways and says to use only those.

sections.title: Encoding and Characters
sections.content:
I-JSON messages MUST be encoded using UTF-8 (RFC 3629). Object member names, and string values in arrays and object members, MUST NOT include code points that identify Surrogates or Noncharacters as defined by the Unicode Standard.

The rule covers characters written directly in UTF-8 and characters written as escapes. The RFC gives an example: \uDEAD is invalid because it is an unpaired surrogate, while \uD800\uDEAD would be legal.
sections.plainLanguage: Everybody must write their letters using the same alphabet code, and some special letter pieces may never be used on their own, like a puzzle piece that only works as half of a pair.

sections.title: Numbers
sections.content:
Software that implements IEEE 754-2008 binary64 (double precision) numbers is generally available and widely used. A sender therefore cannot assume that a receiver can handle numbers with greater magnitude or precision. I-JSON messages SHOULD NOT include numbers that express more magnitude or precision than an IEEE 754 double precision number provides. The RFC's examples are 1E400 and 3.141592653589793238462643383279.

A sender also cannot expect a receiver to treat an integer whose absolute value is greater than 9007199254740991 as exact. That is the range from -(253)+1 to (253)-1.

When an application needs exact numbers beyond those limits, it is RECOMMENDED to encode them in JSON string values. This works only if the receiving program understands what the string means. The RFC's example is 64-bit integers, which modern hardware handles but JavaScript numbers do not, given their limited scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A ruler only has so many tiny marks. If you write a length that needs more marks than the ruler has, the reader will round it. For exact big numbers, write them out as words in a string instead.

sections.title: Object Constraints
sections.content:
Objects in I-JSON messages MUST NOT have members with duplicate names. Here, duplicate means that the names, after processing any escaped characters, are identical sequences of Unicode characters. Two names that look different on the page but decode to the same characters still count as duplicates.

The order of members in an object does not change the meaning of an I-JSON message. A receiving implementation MAY treat two I-JSON messages as equivalent if they differ only in the order of the object members.
sections.plainLanguage: In a list of labeled boxes, no two boxes may have the same label, or nobody knows which one you mean. It also does not matter which box sits first.

sections.title: How Receivers Behave
sections.content:
A major advantage of I-JSON is that receivers can avoid ambiguous semantics in the messages they get. Receivers can reject or otherwise disregard messages that do not meet the I-JSON requirements.

Protocols that use I-JSON can be written so that receivers are required to reject messages that break the constraints, or, in the case of security protocols, not to trust them. Designers of such protocols SHOULD provide a way for the receiver of the erroneous data to signal the problem to the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: If a note is written in a confusing way, the reader is allowed to hand it back and say so, instead of guessing what it means.

sections.title: Recommendations for Protocol Design
sections.content:
I-JSON is designed for use in Internet protocols, and the RFC adds four recommendations for protocol designers.

  • Top level. An I-JSON message can be any JSON value, but some software written to the older RFC 4627 accepts only objects or arrays at the top level. For maximum interoperability, designers SHOULD NOT use top-level texts that are neither objects nor arrays.
  • Must-Ignore. When an implementation meets a protocol element it does not recognize, it treats the rest of the transaction as if the element did not appear, and MUST NOT treat this as an error. The converse Must-Understand policy has proven overly restrictive and brittle in general. A good way to get Must-Ignore is to require top-level elements to be objects and to say that members with unrecognized names MUST be ignored.
  • Time and date. Timestamps and durations are RECOMMENDED to be strings in ISO 8601 format as specified in RFC 3339, with extra restrictions: uppercase letters, an explicit time zone, and optional trailing seconds included even when they are 00. Durations are RECOMMENDED to follow the duration production in Appendix A of RFC 3339, with the same restrictions.
  • Binary data. Arbitrary binary data is RECOMMENDED to be encoded in a string value using base64url, as in Section 5 of RFC 4648.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also gives tips for people who build things with I-JSON: put your data in a box, ignore labels you do not know instead of panicking, write dates one careful way, and turn pictures and files into plain letters first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
All the security considerations that apply to JSON in RFC 7159 apply to I-JSON. The RFC says there are no additional security considerations specific to I-JSON.

Because I-JSON forbids certain JSON idioms that can lead to unpredictable behavior in receiving software, the RFC suggests it may prove a more secure basis for Internet protocols and may be a good choice for designers with special security needs.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything that is risky about JSON is still risky here. But fewer confusing choices means fewer chances for a sneaky trick to slip through.

items.title: Objects or arrays on top
items.text: Avoid top-level texts that are neither, for older parsers.

items.title: Must-Ignore
items.text: Skip unrecognized members instead of failing.

items.title: RFC 3339 strings
items.text: Times and durations as strings, uppercase, with time zone.

items.title: base64url
items.text: Binary data goes in a string using base64url.
